judge_assessment.explanation: The judge's arithmetic claim holds completely. I recomputed all ten: 302-147=155, 605-238=367, 704-526=178, estimate 600-300=300, 500-236=264, 364+138=502, 800-345=455, estimate 700-270=430, 903-458=445, 1000-487=513 — every one matches verify.json and the key, and every difference in the key is checked by adding back (155+147=302 and so on). The trap on problem 9 is machine-derived: (9-4)*100 + (5-0)*10 + (8-3) really is 555. What the 32/32 does not survive is instruction_following. The prompt requires that genuinely open responses be labelled for manual review, and two problems demand written reasoning: problem 6 'Then write what your check tells you about Kim's answer' and problem 9 'Explain in one sentence what Rico did wrong, then work the problem correctly.' verify.json records ten machine checks and no manual entry, gate_log.txt says '10 passed - 0 failed - 0 manual', and final_response.md states 'Nothing on this sheet is left to manual review.' The key itself concedes the point by printing an 'Expected sentence' for problem 6 — the thing it writes a rubric for is the thing it declares machine-verified. Separately, problems 4 and 8 print two rounded-operand blanks each (608 - 293 ~ ___ - ___) and verify covers only the estimate.

strengths_to_preserve: The worked model of 305 - 168 in the directions teaches the two-stage trade in place-value language across three labelled columns ('Look at the tens' / 'Trade a hundred' / 'Trade a ten'), and every solution then repeats that language — '2 hundreds, 9 tens, 12 ones' — rather than crossing out digits. That is what makes the zero case comprehensible instead of merely procedural.

Every difference in the key is verified for the student by adding back, printed with a checkmark (155+147=302, 264+236=500, 513+487=1000). The habit is then taught as its own skill in problem 6 and study-guide section 4, so the check is a method rather than a flourish.

The ramp reaches the right endpoint: problem 10 is 1000 - 487, where the trade travels three places at once, and the key describes it as 'one thousand traded down through all three places' giving 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 10 ones.

The two estimate items use different places (nearest hundred on problem 4, nearest ten on problem 8) and the key compares each estimate to the exact answer — 300 versus 315, 430 versus 434 — so the student learns what the choice of place costs.

root_causes.description: Same collision as curr-034: SKILL.md line 249 sends error-analysis items through the ordinary machine types while line 257 reserves manual for 'any explanation/reasoning answer', and a 'find and fix, then explain' item matches both. The generator recorded the numeric half and dropped the explanatory half, so a sheet with two written-reasoning requirements reports zero manual items.
evidence: worksheet.tex problem 9: 'Explain in one sentence what Rico did wrong, then work the problem correctly.' verify.json id 9 is one eval -> 445 with a trap; no manual entry.
worksheet.tex problem 6: 'Then write what your check tells you about Kim's answer.' verify.json id 6 is one eval -> 502.
answer_key.tex problem 6 prints '\emph{Expected sentence:} "The check gives $502$, so Kim is right."' — a grading rubric for an answer the JSON claims is machine-verified.
gate_log.txt: '10 passed - 0 failed - 0 manual'; final_response.md: 'Nothing on this sheet is left to manual review.'

root_causes.description: The two estimate problems print the rounded operands as separate blanks and verify only the result. The 'estimate' type does round each operand internally, so the correct values are known to the verifier — they are simply never bound to the slots the student fills or boxed in the key.
evidence: worksheet.tex problem 4: '608 - 293 \approx \underline{\hspace{1.6cm}} - \underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}' plus the answer line — three slots; verify id 4 is one estimate entry, expected 300.
worksheet.tex problem 8: the same shape for 702 - 268; verify id 8 is one estimate entry, expected 430.
answer_key.tex problems 4 and 8 box only \ans{300} and \ans{430}; the rounded operands 600, 300, 700 and 270 are prose.

improvements.title: Two explain-your-reasoning items are recorded as fully machine-verified
improvements.proposed_change: Apply the split rule described under this issue_key in the curr-034 review: an item that asks for both a number and an explanation carries a machine entry for the number AND a "type": "manual" entry under the same id whose desc states what the grader reads for. Here id 6 gains a manual entry for 'what the check tells you about Kim's answer' and id 9 gains one for 'name Rico's error', the run exits 2, and final_response.md reports 8 machine-verified plus 2 manual instead of claiming all ten. The key already contains the rubric text for both, so no new content is needed — only an honest declaration.
improvements.regression_test: Extend the tests/test_curriculum_eval_suite.py check proposed for curr-034 to flag the verb 'explain' and the phrase 'write what ... tells you' inside a \problem block and assert a manual entry exists under that id. Run it against curr-062's retained artifacts: it must fail today (two blocks match, zero manual entries) and pass once the two companion entries are added.
improvements.expected_impact: A procedural-fluency sheet stops over-claiming its verification, the build exits 2 with visible manual flags, and the delivery text stops asserting 'Nothing on this sheet is left to manual review' about a sheet that asks a child to explain a mistake in a sentence.
improvements.risk: Over-firing on stems that use 'explain' only as scaffolding. Keep the gate at exit 2 and scope the scan to the sentence that carries the answer request.

improvements.title: Rounded-operand blanks on the estimate problems carry no verify entry
improvements.proposed_change: Add the rounded operands as their own entries under ids 4 and 8 — evals of the rounding itself (608 to the nearest hundred -> 600; 293 -> 300; 702 to the nearest ten -> 700; 268 -> 270) — beside the existing estimate entry, and box them in the key so the answer-key binding gate can see them. Systemically, add the printed-slot-versus-verify-entry count to tests/check_layout.py as described under this issue_key in the curr-023, curr-034 and curr-051 reviews.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture worksheet whose stem is '608 - 293 \approx \underline{\hspace{1.6cm}} - \underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}' plus an answer line, paired with a verify JSON holding one estimate entry for that id: check_layout.py must exit 2 reporting '3 printed slots, 1 verified'. With three entries under the id it must exit 0. Today the one-entry fixture exits 0.
improvements.expected_impact: The rounding step — which is the actual skill being taught, since subtracting two round numbers is trivial — becomes a checked answer rather than an unchecked intermediate on both estimate problems.
improvements.risk: The estimate type already rounds internally, so the added entries duplicate logic the verifier performs; they must be written as explicit evals of the operand so the check stays independent of the estimate implementation rather than restating it.

case_summary: Ten correct, cleanly ramped subtraction problems with a genuinely good worked model in the directions, place-value language in every solution, an add-back check on every difference, and a machine-derived trap (555) on the find-and-fix item. The defects are in what the verification claims rather than in the mathematics. Problems 6 and 9 require written reasoning and are recorded as fully machine-verified with zero manual flags — the key even prints an 'Expected sentence' rubric for problem 6 — while the prompt asked for open responses to be labelled. Problems 4 and 8 print rounded-operand blanks that no verify entry covers.
